title: Voice & Verse
sub: The Literature of the Harlem Renaissance · Grades 5–8 · ELA
objective: Students will analyze the literary techniques of Harlem Renaissance writers, understand how writers used their craft as both art and activism, evaluate primary source texts as historical evidence, and develop their own voice in response to Renaissance themes.
materials: Access to exhibition’s Harlem in Words poetry workshop
Optional: printed or projected excerpts from public domain Harlem Renaissance texts

steps.title: Your voice on paper
script: Write on the board: *“What does your voice sound like on paper?”* Ask students to write for 90 seconds — anything, no rules. Then ask: *“Does your writing sound like YOU, or does it sound like how you think you’re supposed to write?”* This is exactly the question Harlem Renaissance writers were asking.

steps.title: Their own voices
script: *“The writers of the Harlem Renaissance made a radical decision: they would write in their own voices. Not the formal English of white academic tradition. Their own rhythms, their own vernacular, their own truth. Langston Hughes wrote poetry that used the rhythms of jazz and blues. Zora Neale Hurston captured the dialect of Black Southern speech in her novels. They were saying: our way of speaking is not a deficiency. It is literature.”*

steps.title: Art and activism
script: *“This was a political act as much as an artistic one. In a country that told Black Americans their culture was inferior, writing beautiful, powerful, innovative literature was an act of resistance. Every poem published, every novel reviewed in major newspapers, every prize won was evidence that the dominant narrative was wrong.”*

screen.text: Every poem published, every novel reviewed in major newspapers, every prize won was evidence that the dominant narrative was wrong.

steps.purpose: Read the writing as an argument, as well as art.
students: Why was writing beautiful, powerful, innovative literature an act of resistance?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Distribute student handouts. Students self-select their challenge level. Circulate with targeted questions to push thinking at each level.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Scaffolded activities with vocabulary support and structured response frames. Students engage with core content with guidance.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Independent grade-level analysis. Students apply concepts, make connections, and express their own thinking without heavy scaffolding.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Extended critical thinking and research. Students synthesize across sources, evaluate arguments, and produce original analysis or creative work.

steps.purpose: Analyze the writers’ craft, and find a voice of your own, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.

steps.title: Closing
script: Bring the class back together. Ask 2–3 students from different levels to share one thing they discovered or created. Close with:

*“The Harlem Renaissance wasn’t just a historical event. It was a demonstration that ordinary people — with talent, community, and courage — can create something that changes the world. The work you’ve done today connects you to that tradition.”*

screen.text: Ordinary people — with talent, community, and courage — can create something that changes the world.

steps.purpose: Share across the levels, and connect today’s work to the tradition.
students: Share one thing you discovered or created.
Exit ticket: *What is one connection between the Harlem Renaissance and ELA?*
